subject: mathematics
question_text: By using Cramer's rule, solve x + y + z = 1, 2x + 2y + 3z = 6, x + 4y + 9z = 3.

mark_split.label: Write the system as AX = D
Find Δ = det A and check it is not zero
Apply Cramer's rule and state the solution

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Junior Inter Maths-1A (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.28 — LAQ chapter 3 Matrices, answer 18.3. Printed appearances: TS 20 · AP 20. ⚠ THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S. Book pp.27-28 set the Cramer questions two to a page in two columns, which leaves no margin for the [N Marks] tags the chapter uses elsewhere, so no split is printed for any of the four Cramer answers. The 1+1+1+1+1+2 above follows the only split this book states for a solving-a-system question — the note on book p.30 reading 'Just finding A⁻¹ gives u 4 Marks. For remaining steps u get 3 Marks', which weights the bulk computation against the finish. Here that bulk is four determinants, so each carries one mark and the rule plus the answer carry two. A teacher may weight Δ higher, since a zero Δ would make Cramer's rule inapplicable. The SAME split and the SAME step ids are used on all four Cramer answers in this unit, deliberately: the four questions are one method over different numbers. Star rank is the CHAPTER's ★★★, not this question's. Paper position: Maths-1A Section C runs Q18-Q24 at 7 marks each, answer any 5 of 7. Re-cut to the 8-mark Section-C form of the 2026-27 pattern (TGBIE model paper w.e.f. 2026-27): the extra mark goes to the "Apply Cramer's rule and state the solution" step.

recall_prompt: Say how you would solve this by Cramer's rule — say what four determinants you need, how you build each one, and how you get x, y and z at the end.

steps.label: Write it as AX = D
steps.margin_note: First mark. A holds the coefficients in x, y, z order, X holds the unknowns, D holds the right-hand sides. Line the equations up in x, y, z order before building A — a missing term is the commonest error in the whole question.
steps.memory_tip: Line the equations up in x, y, z order so the coefficients land in the right columns.
lines: The system in matrix form is AX = D, where

lines.text: A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 4 & 9 \end{bmatrix}, \ X = \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix}, \ D = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 6 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}

recall.must_convey: That the system is written as AX = D, with A the coefficient matrix, X the column of unknowns and D the column of constants.
accept: write the system as A X equals D where A is the coefficient matrix X is x y z and D is the constants
put it in matrix form with the coefficients in A the unknowns in X and the right hand sides in D
first write A X equals D taking the coefficients into A
modata AX equals D form lo rasta, A lo coefficients, D lo right side values
form the coefficient matrix the variable column and the constant column

steps.why: Cramer's rule is a fixed procedure applied to this matrix. Getting A right is the only place the original equations are used, so every later step inherits any mistake made here.
common_mistakes: Writing the coefficients in the order they appear rather than in x, y, z order.
Missing a coefficient of 1 or −1 because the letter is written with no number in front.
Putting the constants into A instead of D.

steps.label: Find Δ
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Δ is −3 here, a small negative number, so every division at the end flips a sign. That is exactly where this question is lost, and it is why the sign of Δ is worth writing on its own line.
steps.memory_tip: Δ = −3, a NEGATIVE number, so every division at the end flips a sign. That is where this one is lost.

recall.must_convey: That Δ is the determinant of the coefficient matrix, that it works out to −3, and that being non-zero is what allows Cramer's rule to be used.
accept: delta is the determinant of A which comes to minus 3 and since it is not zero cramer's rule can be used
find the determinant of the coefficient matrix and check it is not zero
expand det A and it is non zero so the method works
delta equals det A, zero kaadu kabatti cramer rule use cheyyochu
the determinant of A must be non zero for this rule to apply

steps.why: Cramer's rule divides by Δ. If Δ were zero the division would be impossible and the system would have either no solution or infinitely many — so the check is part of the method, not a formality.
common_mistakes: Computing Δ but never writing that it is non-zero.
Getting the sign pattern wrong when expanding: it is plus, minus, plus along the top row.
Using the constants column somewhere inside Δ.

steps.label: Find Δ₁
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Δ₁ is Δ with the FIRST column replaced by the constants. Columns 2 and 3 are untouched. Replace, never insert.
steps.memory_tip: Δ₁ replaces the first column with the constants, leaving the other two alone.
lines: Replace C₁ of Δ by the constants:

recall.must_convey: That Δ₁ is formed by replacing the FIRST column of Δ with the constants, and that it works out to −21.
accept: delta one is delta with the first column replaced by the constants and it comes to minus 21
put the constants into the first column and expand
replace column one with the right hand side values to get delta one
first column place lo constants pettithe delta one vasthundi
swap the first column for the constant column and expand

steps.why: Δ₁ pairs with x because x is the first unknown. The subscript is a position, not a name — which is why the constants go into column one and nowhere else.
common_mistakes: Replacing a row instead of a column.
Replacing the second column and later dividing it into x.
Adding a fourth column instead of replacing one.

steps.label: Find Δ₂
steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. Same move, second column. Column 1 goes back to the coefficients of x — a common slip is to leave the constants there from the previous step.
steps.memory_tip: Second column now; restore column 1 to the x coefficients first.
lines: Replace C₂ of Δ by the constants:

recall.must_convey: That Δ₂ is formed by replacing the SECOND column of Δ with the constants, and that it works out to 30.
accept: delta two is delta with the second column replaced by the constants and it equals 30
put the constants into the middle column and expand
replace column two with the constant column
second column lo constants pettithe delta two vasthundi
the middle column becomes the constants and then expand

steps.why: Each unknown gets the determinant whose replaced column is that unknown's own column in A. y sits in column two, so Δ₂ is y's determinant.
common_mistakes: Leaving the constants in column one from the previous step, so two columns are wrong at once.
Forgetting the minus in front of the middle term when expanding along the top row.

steps.label: Find Δ₃
steps.margin_note: Fifth mark. Last one — third column replaced, the other two back to the coefficients.
steps.memory_tip: Third column replaced, the other two back to the coefficients.
lines: Replace C₃ of Δ by the constants:

recall.must_convey: That Δ₃ is formed by replacing the THIRD column of Δ with the constants, and that it works out to −12.
accept: delta three is delta with the third column replaced by the constants and it comes to minus 12
put the constants into the last column and expand
replace column three with the constant column
third column lo constants pettithe delta three vasthundi
the last column becomes the constants and then expand

steps.why: Three unknowns need three replaced determinants, plus Δ itself. Four determinants is always the cost of Cramer's rule on a 3×3 system, and knowing that in advance is how you budget the time.
common_mistakes: Stopping after Δ₂ and trying to find z by substitution.
Leaving an earlier replacement in place.

steps.label: Apply Cramer's rule
steps.margin_note: The last three marks, and the only hard part of this question. Δ is NEGATIVE, so a positive Δ₂ gives a negative y. An answer with no negative number in it is wrong here.
steps.memory_tip: Δ is negative, so a positive Δ₂ gives a NEGATIVE y. An answer with no minus in it is wrong.

recall.must_convey: That each unknown is its own determinant divided by Δ, giving x = 7, y = −10, z = 4. The division rule must be stated, not just the answers.
accept: x is delta one by delta y is delta two by delta and z is delta three by delta
divide each of the three determinants by delta to get the three unknowns
by cramer's rule each unknown is its own determinant over delta
prathi determinant ni delta tho divide cheste x y z vasthai
delta one over delta gives x and similarly for y and z

steps.why: The whole method exists so that each unknown can be found on its own, without eliminating anything. That is also why an error in one determinant spoils only one unknown.
common_mistakes: Dividing Δ by Δ₁ instead of Δ₁ by Δ.
Losing a sign when Δ or a numerator is negative.
Never substituting back to check — putting x=7, y=−10, z=4 into the first equation gives 7−10+4 = 1.

insider_note: Δ = −3 is small, so the answers are large: 7, −10 and 4. Substitute them back into all three equations — with numbers this size a slip is easy and the check is quick.
